lines: Imagine you're shipping a box of phones abroad. A hundred kilos, worth fifty thousand dollars. That's about forty-four lakh rupees.
The flight is delayed. Your box sits at the airport for two days, and your buyer wants every rupee back.
So who pays? Let me explain.
Every air shipment travels with a document called an air waybill. Think of it as your cargo's plane ticket.
It's also a contract with the airline: the contract of carriage. It says what the airline promises, and where that promise stops.
Now look at one box on it: declared value for carriage. Most people leave it as N. V. D. No value declared.
Here's the catch. When that box says N, V, D, a global treaty called the Montreal Convention decides what the airline owes you. And it only looks at weight, not value.
The limit is twenty-six S. D. R. per kilo.
S. D. R. stands for Special Drawing Rights: a currency made by the I. M. F. from a basket of world currencies. One S. D. R. is about a hundred and twenty rupees.
So what does that mean in money? For our hundred kilos, about thirty-five hundred dollars. Roughly three lakh rupees, for goods worth forty-four lakh.
What about the delay? It counts, but only for losses you can prove it caused.
And you're on a clock. Complain in writing within twenty-one days, and go to court within two years, or the claim is gone.
So how do you protect yourself? Write the real value in that box and pay an extra fee, and the limit goes up. Or buy cargo insurance, but check it, because most policies don't cover delay.
Which option costs less? That's part two.
Until then, before your cargo flies, check that box. More at F-sixteens e-freight dot com.
